title: 17 countries set out AI priorities for government science research
source_used: Tech Times (same story as the unreadable AI News page; News9live and NBC News also read)
key_facts: On Sunday 4 Oct 2026, at the 23rd annual meeting of the Science and Technology in Society (STS) Forum in Kyoto, the United States and 16 partner countries endorsed the Kyoto Vision declaration, which calls for AI (called 'super intelligence' in the text) to be built into scientific research worldwide (Tech Times).

The 17 signatories are Argentina, Bulgaria, Chile, Cyprus, Germany, Greece, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Kazakhstan, South Korea, New Zealand, Poland, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States; China and India are not among them (Tech Times; News9live gives the same list as named by the White House).

The declaration has three pillars: better institutions and funding for science (long-duration awards, rapid grants, challenge-based funding), harnessing AI for science with wider access to AI, data, computing and facilities, and building scientific talent such as technicians and early-career researchers.

No country pledged money, signed a treaty or accepted an enforcement mechanism; the text uses the word 'endeavor' four times, and the White House announcement said ministers 'pledged' and 'committed', words that do not appear in the declaration itself (Tech Times).
News9live: the document sets no binding targets, budgets or common delivery timetable, and does not say how costs will be divided, how sensitive data will be protected or how access will be governed.
Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, led the US delegation and presented the declaration.
NBC News reported on 3 Oct, before the release, that the United States and 15 other countries would publish the statement; our 4 Oct edition carried that report as item 58.
Tech Times says the forum's closing session on Tuesday (6 Oct) is expected to formally receive the Kyoto Vision as a reference document.
quote_evidence: Seventeen governments aligned around the same agenda; not one of them pledged a dollar, signed a treaty, or accepted an enforcement mechanism.
The White House press release announcing the Kyoto Vision described signatory ministers as having "pledged" and "committed" — but those words do not appear in the published declaration text itself.
It does not set binding targets, budgets or a common delivery timetable.
why_it_matters_hint: A US-led group of 17 governments names AI-run labs and wider access to AI, data and computing as goals for research, but the text commits no money, targets or enforcement, and China and India are outside it.
notes: The AI News page was behind a captcha (HTTP 202). The same story was read on Tech Times (5 Oct 2026, used as the source) and News9live (5 Oct 2026), plus NBC News's 3 Oct advance report (read), which our 4 Oct edition carried as item 58. Tech Times mixes reporting with its own commentary (that 'super intelligence' is a political label, the count of 'endeavor'); only attributed facts are used. NBC expected the US and 15 other countries; the final count is 17 in all, the US plus 16.
